rows.stem: In the ring structure of fructose, the anomeric carbon is
rows.solution: The anomeric carbon is the one that becomes a new stereocentre when the open chain closes into its cyclic hemiacetal or hemiketal form — that is, the carbonyl carbon of the open chain. In an aldose such as glucose the carbonyl is the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) at C-1, so C-1 is the anomeric carbon. Fructose is a KETOSE: its carbonyl is a keto group at C-2. When the ring closes, it is therefore C-2 that acquires the new hydroxyl and the new configuration, so C-2 is the anomeric carbon in fructose.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Which of the following is the correct expression of \(\mathrm{K_f}\) which depends upon the nature of solvent ?
rows.solution:
The cryoscopic constant is a property of the solvent alone, so its expression can contain only solvent quantities: the molar mass of the solvent \(M_1\), its normal freezing point \(T_f\), and its enthalpy of fusion \(\Delta_{fus}H\), together with the gas constant. The correct relation is
\(K_f = \dfrac{R \times M_1 \times T_f^2}{1000 \times \Delta_{fus}H}\)

Two checks confirm it without memorising. The freezing point appears SQUARED, and the enthalpy of fusion is in the DENOMINATOR — a solvent that resists melting strongly has a small \(K_f\). The factor of 1000 converts the molar mass from grams to kilograms so that the constant suits molality.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following transition metals has lowest enthalpy of atomisation ?
rows.solution:
Enthalpy of atomisation measures how much energy is needed to break the metal apart into free atoms, so it measures the strength of the metallic bonding — which depends on how many unpaired d electrons each atom contributes.

Chromium (\(3d^5 4s^1\)), vanadium (\(3d^3 4s^2\)) and iron (\(3d^6 4s^2\)) all have several electrons available for bonding. Manganese is \(3d^5 4s^2\): its half-filled \(3d^5\) subshell is unusually stable and its \(4s\) electrons are paired, so its electrons are held within the atom rather than shared between atoms. Fewer electrons take part in the metallic bonding, so manganese has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation in the series.

rows.stem: The secondary valency of Co in \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) is
rows.solution:
The secondary valency is the coordination number, the number of ligand donor ATOMS bonded directly to the metal. Ethane-1,2-diamine is BIDENTATE: each molecule donates through two nitrogen atoms. Three of them therefore supply six donor atoms, and the secondary valency of cobalt in \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) is 6.

Counting ligand molecules instead of donor atoms gives 3, which is one of the choices offered — and which happens to be the PRIMARY valency here, the oxidation state of the cobalt.

rows.stem: At low temperature, phenol on reaction with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) in \(\mathrm{CS_2}\) gives
rows.solution:
Bromination of phenol is a case where the conditions decide how far the reaction goes. In a non-polar solvent such as carbon disulphide, and at low temperature, phenol is not ionised, so the ring is activated but only moderately, and a single bromine enters. It enters at both the available activated positions, so the product is a mixture of ortho-bromophenol and para-bromophenol, which are separated afterwards.

Bromine WATER is the contrasting case: there phenol ionises to the far more strongly activated phenoxide, all three positions are brominated at once, and 2,4,6-tribromophenol precipitates immediately.

rows.stem: How the conductivity varies on decreasing concentration for both weak and strong electrolytes ?

options.label: A
options.text: It increases for weak electrolyte and decreases for strong electrolyte.

options.label: B
options.text: It decreases for weak electrolyte and increases for strong electrolyte.

options.label: C
options.text: It increases for both weak and strong electrolytes.

options.label: D
options.text: It decreases for both weak and strong electrolytes.

rows.solution:
Conductivity, \(\kappa\), is the conductance of a unit volume of solution, so it depends on how many ions that volume contains. Diluting a solution spreads the same number of ions through a larger volume, so any given volume holds fewer of them and the conductivity falls. This is true for a strong electrolyte and for a weak one alike, so conductivity decreases for both.

The property that behaves differently is MOLAR conductivity, \(\Lambda_m\), which is conductivity divided by concentration. That rises on dilution, gently for a strong electrolyte because the ions interfere with one another less, and steeply for a weak one because more of it dissociates.

rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — options (C) and (D) are printed as two-dimensional condensed structural formulae: the carbonyl carbon sits on the chain line with a drawn vertical double bond BELOW it and the O below that. The LaTeX above reproduces that layout with \underset rather than approximating it, so the row is answerable from text alone; options (A) and (B) are ordinary linear formulae. Read on my own page at 5x. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
Acetic anhydride acylates a primary amine at nitrogen. One acetyl group is transferred and acetic acid is released, so the amine becomes a substituted amide:
\(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2} + (\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-NH-CO-CH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)
The product is N-methylacetamide. Note that the nitrogen keeps its methyl group and gains an acetyl one — it is not replaced, which is what the plain acetamide choice would require.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The activation energy of a reaction can be determined from the slope of which of the following curves ?
rows.solution:
Take logarithms of the Arrhenius equation \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\):
\(\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T}\)

This has the form \(y = c + mx\) with \(y = \ln k\) and \(x = 1/T\). So plotting \(\ln k\) against \(1/T\) gives a straight line whose slope is \(-E_a/R\), and the activation energy follows as \(E_a = -R \times \text{slope}\).

Plotting \(\ln k\) against \(T\) itself would not be linear, because the temperature enters as its reciprocal.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Identify ‘X’ in the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{CH_3 - \underset{\mathrm{O}}{\underset{\|}{\mathrm{C}}} - CH_2 - \underset{\mathrm{O}}{\underset{\|}{\mathrm{C}}} - O - CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaBH_4}} \text{‘X’}\)
‘X’ is
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — the substrate and options (A)–(D) are printed as two-dimensional condensed structural formulae: each carbonyl O is drawn BELOW its carbon on a vertical double bond, and each –OH BELOW its carbon on a vertical single bond. The LaTeX above reproduces that layout with \underset rather than approximating it, so the row is answerable from text alone. The compound is deliberately NOT named in words anywhere on this row, because naming it would state the answer. Read on my own page at 5x. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
Sodium borohydride is a mild reducing agent. It reduces aldehydes and ketones but NOT esters, which are far less electrophilic because the ester oxygen donates electron density into the carbonyl by resonance.

The compound here has both: a ketone at one end and a methyl ester at the other. Only the ketone is attacked, and it becomes a secondary alcohol while the ester survives untouched:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_2-COOCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaBH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-COOCH_3}\)
The choices that reduce the ester as well would need a stronger reagent such as lithium aluminium hydride, which is exactly the distinction being tested.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The presence of –OH group in phenols directs the incoming group at ortho- and para- positions.
Reason (R) : –OH group in phenols deactivates the aromatic ring.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group does direct incoming electrophiles to the ortho and para positions, so the Assertion is true.

The Reason has the effect backwards. By donating its lone pair into the ring, \(-\mathrm{OH}\) raises the ring's electron density and makes phenol far MORE reactive than benzene towards electrophiles — it ACTIVATES the ring, it does not deactivate it. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Actinoids show irregularities in their electronic configurations.
Reason (R) : Due to varying stabilities of \(\mathrm{f^0}\), \(\mathrm{f^7}\) and \(\mathrm{f^{14}}\) occupancies of the 5f orbitals.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Actinoids do show irregular electronic configurations, so the Assertion is true, and the Reason names the cause correctly. A subshell that is empty, exactly half filled or completely filled has extra stability, so the \(5f^0\), \(5f^7\) and \(5f^{14}\) occupancies are favoured. Near those points an electron will sometimes sit in a 6d orbital instead of the 5f orbital the ordinary filling order predicts, and that is what the irregularities are.

Both statements are true, and the second is the reason for the first, so the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The pentaacetate of glucose does not react with \(\mathrm{H_2N - OH}\).
Reason (R) : It indicates the absence of free –CHO group in glucose.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Glucose pentaacetate has all five hydroxyl groups acetylated, and it does not react with hydroxylamine, so the Assertion is true. Hydroxylamine reacts with a free \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group to give an oxime, so a failure to react is evidence that no free \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group is present — which is exactly what the Reason states, so it is true too.

The one follows from the other directly: the absence of reaction IS the evidence for the absence of the free aldehyde group. So the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion. This observation is one of the pieces of evidence that forced the cyclic hemiacetal structure of glucose.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : It is not possible to separate the components of an azeotrope by fractional distillation.
Reason (R) : Minimum boiling azeotrope is formed by the solutions showing large positive deviation from Raoult’s law.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The components of an azeotrope cannot be separated by fractional distillation, so the Assertion is true. Minimum boiling azeotropes are indeed formed by solutions showing large positive deviation from Raoult's law, so the Reason is true as well.

But the Reason explains only how ONE KIND of azeotrope comes about; it says nothing about why separation fails. The reason separation fails is that the vapour has the same composition as the liquid, so repeated vaporisation cannot enrich it — and that applies to maximum boiling azeotropes too, which come from negative deviation. So both are true but the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem: What type of deviation is shown by a mixture of chloroform and acetone from Raoult’s law ? Give reason. What will happen to the boiling point of the solution on mixing chloroform and acetone ?
rows.solution:
A mixture of chloroform and acetone shows negative deviation from Raoult's law. The hydrogen atom of chloroform is made unusually acidic by the three chlorine atoms pulling electron density away from it, so it forms a hydrogen bond to the carbonyl oxygen of acetone. That new chloroform-to-acetone interaction is stronger than the chloroform-chloroform and acetone-acetone interactions it replaces, so after mixing the molecules are held in the liquid more tightly than before. Fewer escape, each partial vapour pressure falls below the value Raoult's law predicts, and the total vapour pressure of the mixture is lowered.

Because the vapour pressure has been lowered, the mixture must be heated further before it can match the external pressure. The boiling point of the solution therefore increases.

rows.stem:
Differentiate between the following :
(i) Fibrous protein and Globular protein
(ii) Peptide linkage and Phosphodiester linkage
rows.solution:
(i) In a fibrous protein the polypeptide chains lie parallel to one another and are held side by side by hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges, giving a thread-like structure that is insoluble in water; keratin and myosin are examples. In a globular protein the chain coils and folds back on itself into a roughly spherical shape, and these are generally soluble in water; insulin and albumin are examples.

(ii) A peptide linkage is the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CONH}-\) formed when the \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) of one amino acid condenses with the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) of the next; it joins amino acid residues into a protein. A phosphodiester linkage is the bridge formed when a phosphate group esterifies the sugars of two neighbouring nucleotides; it joins nucleotides into a nucleic acid. So one builds proteins and the other builds DNA and RNA, and the atoms involved are quite different — nitrogen and carbon in one, phosphorus and oxygen in the other.

rows.stem:
How do you explain the presence of following in open structure of glucose ?
(a) all the six carbon atoms are in a straight chain.
(b) five –OH groups which are attached to different carbon atoms.
(c) an aldehyde group.
rows.solution:
Each of the three features was established by a particular reaction, and the reaction is the evidence.

(a) The straight chain of six carbons. Heated for a long time with hydriodic acid, glucose is reduced completely — every oxygen is stripped away — and what is left is \(n\)-hexane, the unbranched hydrocarbon:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HI},\ \Delta} \mathrm{CH_3(CH_2)_4CH_3}\)
Since the carbon skeleton cannot rearrange under these conditions, the six carbons must already have been in a straight chain.

(b) The five hydroxyl groups on five different carbons. Glucose reacts with acetic anhydride to give a stable pentaacetate, a derivative carrying exactly five acetyl groups. Acetylation occurs at hydroxyl groups, so there are five of them:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{CHO(CH{-}OCOCH_3)_4CH_2{-}OCOCH_3}\)
That they sit on five DIFFERENT carbons follows from the compound being stable: two hydroxyl groups on one carbon would make a gem-diol, which loses water at once.

(c) The aldehyde group. Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent that attacks an aldehyde group and nothing else, and it converts glucose to the six-carbon gluconic acid:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2\ water}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
A ketone would not be oxidised under these conditions, so the carbonyl must be an aldehyde. Forming an oxime with hydroxylamine and a cyanohydrin with hydrogen cyanide is further evidence of the same group.
